newsitem.title: USA: US Treasury official sees little inflation risk.
newsitem.headline: US Treasury official sees little inflation risk.

text.p: A senior Treasury Department official said on Tuesday that there was little sign of demand-induced inflation pressures in the steadily growing U.S. economy.

"The evidence for any appreciable risk currently from demand-side inflation is merager to non-existent," John Auten, director of Treasury's Office of Financial Analysis, told private-sector members of the Public Securities Association that advises Treasury on its borrowing requirements.
Mild winter weather probably helped the economy expand at around a four percent annual rate in the first quarter, he said.

But Auten said there could be "statistical payback" in the current quarter because construction activity and consumer spending that occurred in the first quarter may effectively take away from second-quarter growth.

"If so, growth could even now be returning much closer to trend," Auten said, adding there were "few signs that the recent burst of economic growth will necessarily become self-reinforcing or that it signals a new, more inflationary, phase of the current expansion."
Treasury said on Monday it intends to pay down the government's debt by $65 billion in the second quarter.

Paul Malvey, associate director of Treasury's Office of Market Finance, said the big paydown in government debt was possible because of "an unexpectedly large surge in tax receipts" from individuals meeting 1996 obligations.
"This has even surprised our receipt analysts," he said.
Malvey said foreign investor interest in U.S. Treasury securities was "still strong, ballooning by another $46.5 billion in the first two months of the first quarter.
"And there is some evidence that suggests that the heavy foreign purchases continued beyond the end of February," he added.
Foreign buying of U.S. Treasury secuirities is rising at a 20 percent annual clip so far this year compared with a 23 percent gain in 1996 and a 22 percent gain in 1995.

Foreign holdings as a percentage of total U.S. government debt hit 32 percent at the the end of 1996, Malvey said. Japan has increased its holdings of U.S. securities at a 28 percent annual rate so far in 1997 compared with a 26 percent increase in 1996.
Malvey noted a 75 percent to 78 percent pickup in buying of U.S. Treasury securities by Hong Kong residents in 1996.
Treasury has set a news conference for 1:00 p.m. EDT (1700 GMT) on Wednesday to detail its plans for selling three- and 10-year notes next week to meet its second-quarter financial objectives.
